TextBlock.Text: Saturday, 22 April 2028 | European Edition | No. 21,890 | 2.80 EUR

StackPanel.TextBlock:
KATTEGAT — At 2140 last night, aboard a frigate somewhere between Jutland and Sweden, a signalman hauled down a flag that had flown from that mast for four years, and ran up one that nobody had ever seen before.
The transmission that followed lasted forty seconds and was made in clear, so that every merchant ship, every coastguard station and every newsroom on the Baltic could hear it. “We are no longer asking,” Konteradmiral Reimar Vahl said. “We are no longer subject to any authority that will not exercise itself.”
Until last night the legal position had been, at worst, ambiguous. A commander in disobedience of orders is a matter for a court martial. A commander under his own ensign is something for which nobody in Brussels has a word ready.
What happened after the transmission was less symbolic. Three submarines of the Type 212A class, which had been unaccounted for since 11 April, were reported by coastal sonar arrays moving south into the central Kattegat: forty metres of water, heavy bottom clutter, and the worst hunting ground in Europe for the people who will have to go and find them.
A NATO spokesperson confirmed that Task Group NORTHWIND has been ordered into the Kattegat and declined all further comment.

The three merchant ships detained in the northern Kattegat since 18 April are clear and proceeding north. All 410 people aboard are accounted for.
The master of the NORDLAND, asked what the last four days had been like, said only that the weather had been fine.

The North Atlantic Council has now met eleven times since the sabotage of the eastern Baltic interconnectors on 9 March.
It has agreed on the wording of four communiques.
